what_its_for: Rituximab-abbs is used to treat certain types of cancer (like non-Hodgkin's lymphoma and chronic lymphocytic leukemia) and autoimmune diseases (like rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and microscopic polyangiitis). It works by targeting and destroying certain white blood cells called B-cells that are either cancerous or causing harm to your body.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an IV (intravenous) infusion — meaning it goes directly into your vein through a needle or catheter. A nurse or doctor will give it to you in a clinic or hospital setting. You will NOT give this to yourself at home. Each infusion can take several hours, so plan to be at the clinic for most of the day. You will be watched closely during and after the infusion for any reactions.
dosing: Your dose depends on your weight, your specific condition, and your doctor's plan for you. It is usually given once a week for 4 doses, or once every 2 to 3 weeks, or on a schedule your doctor sets. Never try to adjust your dose on your own — always follow your care team's instructions exactly.
missed_dose: Since this medicine is given by a healthcare provider, missing a dose is uncommon. However, if you miss or need to reschedule an appointment, call your doctor or clinic as soon as possible. Do NOT try to 'make up' for a missed dose on your own — your care team will decide the best plan.
storage: You do not store this medicine at home. The clinic or hospital pharmacy handles storage. If you are ever given information about storing it, keep it refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C), protect it from light, and do NOT freeze it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid being around people who are sick or have infections, since this medicine lowers your ability to fight germs. Avoid live vaccines (like the live flu nasal spray, MMR, chickenpox, or shingles vaccine) during treatment and for a period after — ask your doctor before getting any vaccines. Avoid alcohol if your doctor recommends it. Tell your doctor before any surgery or dental procedures.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room RIGHT AWAY if you notice: difficulty breathing, chest pain, or tightness during or after an infusion; sudden swelling of your face, lips, or throat; severe skin rash or blistering; signs of infection such as fever over 100.4°F, chills, cough, or painful urination; unusual bleeding or bruising; confusion, weakness on one side of your body, or vision changes (which could be signs of a rare but serious brain infection called PML); stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, or yellowing of the skin or eyes. These could be signs of serious or life-threatening reactions.
when_it_works: It may take several weeks to months before you notice improvement. For cancer, your doctor will use lab tests and scans to check your progress. For conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, many patients notice reduced joint pain and swelling within 3 to 6 months. Everyone is different, so be patient and keep all follow-up appointments.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: This medicine can harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 12 months after your last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 6 months after your last dose. Tell your doctor immediately if you become pregnant. Elderly patients (65 and older): You may have a higher risk of side effects, so your doctor will monitor you closely. Children: Safety and dosing in children varies by condition — follow your pediatric specialist's guidance exactly. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor about any kidney or liver issues before starting treatment.
